title: QRCodeClear
question: How does a QR code work?
hook: A QR code is a tiny page of text, a repair kit and three squares that say where to look. Build one, scratch it and watch a real scanner read it.

explainer.title: Squares are bits
explainer.text: A QR code is a grid of dark and light squares called modules. Each one is a single bit. Version 1 is 21 by 21, and each version adds 4 squares a side, up to 177 by 177 at version 40.

explainer.title: Three squares say where to look
explainer.text: The big squares in three corners show a dark, light, dark, light, dark pattern in the ratio 1 : 1 : 3 : 1 : 1. It looks the same along any line through the middle, so a camera can spot it at any angle. Timing stripes and alignment targets help it count and straighten the grid.

explainer.title: Text becomes bytes, then a zig-zag
explainer.text: The encoder packs your text as digits, capital letters or bytes, pads it, adds check bytes, and lays the bits into the grid two columns at a time. A fixed mask then flips some squares so there are no big blank patches or false finder patterns.

explainer.title: It repairs itself
explainer.text: Reed-Solomon check bytes let a reader find and fix wrong bytes. The four levels, L, M, Q and H, can repair roughly 7, 15, 25 and 30 percent of the code. That is why a scratch, or a small logo in the middle, does not stop it reading.

explainer.title: A phone reads it in four steps
explainer.text: It turns the picture black and white, hunts for the three finder squares, straightens the tilt with a perspective transform, and samples the middle of every module once. Then the decoder fixes any wrong bytes and reads the text.

explainer.title: It only holds text
explainer.text: A code can't run anything by itself. It holds a web address, a Wi-Fi password or a phone number. Fake stickers pasted over real codes, called quishing, work by sending you to the wrong address, so read the address before you tap.

concepts.def: One square of a QR code, dark or light. It is one bit.
The size of the code, from 1 (21 × 21) to 40 (177 × 177). Size is 17 + 4 × version.
The 7 × 7 nested square in three corners. Its 1 : 1 : 3 : 1 : 1 ratio lets a camera find the code at any angle.
A row and a column of alternating modules between the finders, used to count the grid.
A small 5 × 5 target in codes from version 2 up that helps fix perspective and bending.
The blank border around the code, at least 4 modules wide, so the reader can tell where it ends.
How characters are packed into bits: numeric, alphanumeric or byte.
One of 8 fixed patterns of flipped modules that breaks up blank patches and look-alike finders. The best of 8 is chosen.
A way to add check bytes so a receiver can find and fix wrong bytes without a resend.
L, M, Q or H: how many check bytes the code carries, roughly 7, 15, 25 or 30 percent of its bytes.
Phishing through a QR code: a fake code sends you to a page that steals logins or card numbers.

storage.what: Which chapters you have opened, your best quiz scores, and sound on or off.
